budget_note: Report is at its ship-gate length ceiling; every finding below is scoped to a table row, a table cell, or a clause, and each names a displacement candidate. Findings 8 and 9 free words rather than spend them.

findings.location: Section 1A, 'What has been measured' table (add one row) + one clause after the paragraph beginning 'The Kässi figures cover freelancing marketplaces'
findings.issue: The report's opening sentence asserts attrition has 'four measurements counting four different units and no platform-scale survival curve.' The corpus holds a fifth measurement the report never touches, and it is the only platform-scale creator-count time series in the vault that shows net contraction: a census-style Graphtreon scrape of public Patreon pages. This is not a survival curve, but it is a platform-wide net-attrition signal at the same unit (creator with at least one paying member) with a nine-year baseline, and it is the most recent evidence in the entire corpus (Feb 2026). Its omission means the report's audited absence in Section 1B ('the missing measurement is withheld rather than unfound') is stated without disclosing that a census workaround exists and has produced a result.
findings.evidence: [[patreon-subscriber-and-creator-statistics-for-2026]] — Graphtreon census of public Patreon pages plus Patreon company disclosures. Paid-creator count 25,646 (Feb 2017) -> 172,176 (Feb 2022) -> 242,878 (Feb 2024) -> 279,566 (Nov 2024) -> peak 295,083 (Oct 2025) -> 286,287 (Feb 2026): a fall of 8,796 (~3%) in four months, the first contraction after nine years of monotonic growth. Note's own caveat, which must travel with the figure: the metric counts creators with at least one PAYING member, so it cannot separate quitting from losing one's last patron; and Graphtreon covers only creators with visible earnings. Same note: only 31 of 286,287 creators (~0.011%, 1 in 9,200) have over 20,000 paying members.
findings.recommendation: Add one row to the Section 1A table: Finding = 'Net paid-creator count, first contraction' / Value = '295,083 (Oct 2025) -> 286,287 (Feb 2026), -3% in 4 months, after 25,646 in Feb 2017' / Unit = 'Creator with >=1 paying member' / n = 'census, 286,287' / Window = 'Feb 2017 - Feb 2026' / Platform = 'Patreon' / Country = 'Not reported, US-headquartered'. Then extend the existing paragraph at line 23 with one clause stating that this is a net count and therefore conflates exit with loss of a last patron, so it bounds attrition from below rather than measuring it. Displacement: the third sentence of Section 1B on the creatormap vendor exclusion (from 'One vendor source claiming to be this telemetry is excluded' onward) can be cut to a single clause, since Section 6D already carries the fabricated-apparatus argument at length.

findings.location: Section 2A table (add one row) + one sentence in Section 2B or at the end of Section 2A
findings.issue: OnlyFans and Substack are both named as required entities in the decomposition ('OnlyFans / subscription-content platforms', 'Patreon / Substack / direct-support platforms'). Neither word appears anywhere in the report — zero occurrences of 'OnlyFans', zero of 'Substack'. This is not a defensible silent omission, because the corpus contains an audited primary-source aggregate for OnlyFans of exactly the type the report already accepts for YouTube (Rieder: disclosed payout divided by crawled channel count). The report also never states that these platforms were checked, which the run's provenance discipline requires for any audited absence.
findings.evidence: [[onlyfans-creator-income-distribution-report-2026]] — the aggregate traces to Fenix International Ltd's audited UK Companies House filing: gross fan payments $7.22bn FY2024, creator payouts ~80% = $5.80bn, over ~4.63m registered accounts including dormant ones, giving a mean of $1,253/yr; the note observes that this mean sits ABOVE the estimated top-25% threshold (~$1,050), so more than 75% of accounts never reach the average. Also measured: a scrape of n=100,200 public creator profiles, June 2026, top 1% hold 35.5% of likes, top 10% hold 82%, bottom 50% ~0.2% (likes, not dollars). The note's audit verdict is that every circulating OnlyFans PERCENTILE (median ~$180/yr, top 0.1% ~13% of payouts) is sourced only to an unnamed '[PANEL-2024] third-party panel analyses (estimated)' with no sample size, method or date, and drifts between aggregators; corroborated by [[average-onlyfans-income-2026-real-numbers-sirency]], a creator-management agency publishing a conflicting median as a sales asset. Substack: [[how-much-does-substack-cost-substack-inc]] is the only recoverable Substack primary source in the corpus and carries only the 10% platform fee, no income distribution.
findings.recommendation: Add one row to the Section 2A median/mean table: Dataset = 'OnlyFans, Fenix International audited filing' / Median = 'none traceable to any study' / Mean = '$1,253/yr ($5.80bn payouts / 4.63m registered accounts)' / Ratio = 'not computable' / Unit = 'Registered account, incl. dormant' / n = '~4.63m' / Period = 'FY2024' / Platform = 'OnlyFans' / Country = 'Not disclosed'. Add one sentence noting that the circulating OnlyFans percentiles trace to affiliate aggregators citing an unnamed panel, and that no income distribution for Substack was located, only its 10% fee — i.e. state the audited absence explicitly rather than omitting the platforms. Displacement: the report can absorb this by tightening the four-sentence paragraph at line 52 explaining why the three Patreon medians differ, which restates the inclusion-floor point the table's 'Unit / denominator' column already carries.

findings.location: Section 2A table, Twitch row (fill the empty 'Mean' and 'Ratio' cells) + one clause in the Twitch caveat paragraph at line 54
findings.issue: The decomposition requires 'Median AND mean reported side by side wherever income is discussed.' The Twitch row in Section 2A carries a median ('under $28') and no mean, with an em-dash in the Ratio column. The corpus supplies the missing mean from Twitch's own disclosures — and it is the only Twitch figure in the vault with a platform-stated denominator, which is directly responsive to the report's own complaint in Section 6B that the leak's denominator is 'stated at least six incompatible ways.' The report identifies the denominator problem and then does not use the one source that solves it.
findings.evidence: [[twitch-partner-plus-will-pay-70-of-subscription-revenue-to-creators]] (Variety, 15 Jun 2023) — Twitch states it paid out more than $1 billion to streamers in 2022 and that approximately 7 million streamers go live each month, giving a mean of roughly $143 per monthly-active streamer per year, against a leak-derived median of under $28 per earning account over Jan-Sep 2021. Same source: the Partner Plus tier (effective 1 Oct 2023) requires 350 recurring paid subscriptions held for three consecutive months to raise the split from 50/50 to 70/30, and only on the first $100,000 in 12 months — implying roughly $1,200/month gross at the qualifying gate, i.e. Twitch's own elevated tier does not by itself reach a US living wage. Both are company self-disclosures with no methodology, no country breakdown and no definition of 'streamer'. Corroborating concentration figures also uncited: [[twitch-streamers-respond-after-huge-leak-of-creator-payout-data-techcrunch]] (10% of the top 10,000 take 49% of streamer earnings) and [[twitch-leak-10-biggest-revelations-from-the-unprecedented-data-breach]] (rank 10,000 earned $26,000 CUMULATIVELY across the ~26-month leak window).
findings.recommendation: Fill the Twitch row's Mean cell with '~$143/yr per monthly-active streamer ($1bn+ 2022 payouts / ~7m monthly live streamers, platform-disclosed)' and set the Unit cell to note that the mean and median have different denominators (all monthly-active streamers vs earning accounts only) so the ratio is not computable. Add a single clause to the line 54 paragraph recording the 350-subscription Partner Plus gate as a platform-disclosed threshold for a commercially serious creator that still implies roughly $1,200/month gross. This is a table-cell edit plus one clause; no displacement needed beyond the tightening in finding 8.

findings.location: Section 2A table (one row) or the paragraph at line 71 that names Gini as a defensible comparison class
findings.issue: Section 2B closes by ruling that only two comparison classes survive — within-instrument time series holding the denominator constant, and dimensionless shape statistics (mean/median ratios, Gini, Pareto alpha, hazard ratios). The report then supplies exactly one Gini in the whole document (US independent artists, 0.582 vs national 0.474) and no within-platform inequality time series at all. The corpus holds precisely the artefact the report's own methodological rule asks for: a measured Gini series computed on a complete platform transaction record with a constant denominator across six years. This is the highest evidence-per-word omission in the income section, and the source is a peer-reviewed ICWSM paper on the largest creator-payments dataset in the published literature — entirely uncited.
findings.evidence: [[quantifying-the-creator-economy-a-large-scale-analysis-of-patreon]] — El Sanyoura & Anderson (University of Toronto), ICWSM 2022, DOI 10.1609/icwsm.v16i1.19338. Sample: the COMPLETE set of Patreon pledge transactions from platform inception June 2013 to December 2020, hundreds of millions of patron-creator transactions totalling over USD 2 billion paid to creators — administrative platform data, not survey. Findings: within-topic creator Gini rose from 0.30 (2015) to 0.60 (Dec 2020); ACROSS topics inequality fell slightly, 0.80 (mid-2015) to 0.72 (2020) — the platform diversified into more subject areas while concentrating earnings inside each one. Top-decile creators receive nearly $15 per pledge versus $2 for bottom-decile, so high earners win on both audience size and price per patron. Note's own limits, which must travel: no median earnings figure, no attrition rate, no time-to-first-income, no country breakdown; Patreon's base is heavily US/Western.
findings.recommendation: Add one row to the Section 2A table (Dataset = 'El Sanyoura & Anderson, complete Patreon record' / Median = 'not reported' / Mean = 'not reported' / Ratio = 'within-topic Gini 0.30 (2015) -> 0.60 (Dec 2020); cross-topic 0.80 -> 0.72' / Unit = 'Creator, all pledge transactions' / n = 'complete record, >$2bn' / Period = 'Jun 2013 - Dec 2020' / Platform = 'Patreon' / Country = 'Not reported, US-skewed'), or if a row is too costly, add one clause to the line 71 paragraph citing it as the only extant example of the within-instrument time series the paragraph demands. Prefer the row: it also demonstrates that the report's two surviving comparison classes are satisfiable, not merely stipulated.

findings.location: Section 5B, 'Four measured mechanisms of non-transfer' — one clause; or Section 5A scope-flag table, one row
findings.issue: The report contains zero mentions of China or Chinese platforms. The query asks the report to flag which findings are US/Western-only and may not generalise to Southeast Asia; the sharpest way to test that is a middle-income, non-Western, non-SEA Asian income distribution, and the corpus holds four such sources (livestreaming, Zhihu, Xiaohongshu, Bilibili) of which none is cited. Section 5B currently argues non-transfer from Western thresholds, RPM differentials, link infrastructure and informality rates — all mechanism arguments. A directly observed non-Western distribution would show the shape argument empirically instead of by inference, and it happens to land almost exactly on the ADBI living-wage denominator the same section already uses.
findings.evidence: [[chinas-livestreaming-industry-platforms-politics-and-precarity]] — Cunningham, Craig & Lv (2019), International Journal of Cultural Studies 22(6), QUT ePrints accepted manuscript. Citing a Tencent Research Institute report via Meng (2017b): among Chinese livestreamers 'only 5 per cent made more than 10,000 yuan ($1500 USD) a month, while ... more than 70 per cent said they earned less than 100 yuan ($15 USD) a month', set against a reported population of ~3.5 million commercial livestreamers. The note attaches an explicit provenance warning: this is a second-hand citation of an industry report, with no stated methodology, sample size or sampling frame — cite as an industry estimate, not a measured distribution. The paper's own empirical base is qualitative (22 interviewees, Beijing/Shanghai/Guangzhou, 2017, snowball via platform gatekeepers, survivor-skewed). Adjacent uncited China material: [[from-live-to-recording-consumer-demand-and-response-to-price]] (complete Zhihu Live transaction records, May 2016 - Jun 2017) and [[stop-updating-a-textual-analysis-of-chinese-viewers]] (1,176 Bilibili comments, Aug 2023, on the 2023 'stop updating' wave in which vloggers with 10,000 to 3m+ followers publicly announced they would cease uploading).
findings.recommendation: Add one clause to the Section 5B living-wage sentence: that the only non-Western distribution located outside SEA — an industry estimate for ~3.5m Chinese livestreamers, 5% above ~$1,500/month and over 70% below ~$15/month — puts the modal earner roughly seventeen times below the ADBI developing-Asia absolute living wage of $254.28/month, and must be labelled an unmethodologised industry estimate rather than a measurement. Displacement: the parenthetical gloss on 'regression-discontinuity companion' and similar inline method definitions in Section 4B can be shortened, since the report already glosses the same technique earlier.

findings.issue: Imbalanced coverage of a peer approach. Section 1C offers two analogue literatures and both are UNPAID contributors (Wikipedia newcomers, Debian maintainers). The corpus holds the paid-work analogue — a cohort survival curve computed on platform administrative data with an explicit operational stopping rule — and the report drops it entirely, even though Uber appears five times elsewhere in the draft. This matters beyond coverage: the report's central complaint is that no one has published 'N creators started, M remained after t months' with a rule for when someone has stopped. Hall & Krueger is the closest published template for exactly that design, including the stopping rule the report says the field lacks, and it was produced by the platform itself — which is the report's own argument about who holds the missing data.
findings.evidence: [[an-analysis-of-the-labor-market-for-ubers-driver-partners-in-the]] — Hall & Krueger, NBER WP w22843 / ILR Review 2018, using Uber's own administrative trip data. Among 11,267 US UberBLACK/uberX driver-partners who made their first trip between January and June 2013 and had made at least 4 trips: 11% became inactive within one month of starting; 70% were still active after 6 months; more than 50% remained active a full year after starting. Inactivity operationalised as recording no trip for 6+ months. Earnings per hour show a quadratic relationship with tenure, peaking around 14 months. Caveats the note requires: descriptive, not causal; Hall was an Uber employee/shareholder and Krueger a paid Uber consultant during drafting, and Berg & Johnston (2019, ILR Review) contest the framing; ride-hailing exit mechanics differ from creator exit mechanics.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to Section 1C alongside the Wikipedia and Debian figures: Uber's administrative cohort (n=11,267 US drivers, first trip Jan-Jun 2013) gives 11% inactive at one month, 70% active at six, over 50% at twelve, with inactivity defined as no trip in 6+ months — the only published cohort curve on a paid platform, produced by the platform, with the author conflict of interest and the population difference stated in the same clause. Displacement: the Debian sentence's aside about the maintainer population growing to 'about 1,237' can be compressed.

findings.location: Section 5D 'The rest of the regional record' table (Philippines and Indonesia rows) or Section 5B
findings.issue: Layer 1's coverage check named five items as the entirety of genuine SEA quantitative evidence in the corpus; PIDS on Philippine/Indonesian online-workforce composition was one of them and the report cites none of it. The Philippines row in Section 5D currently reads 'Creative-economy aggregates at the wrong unit' and carries only the ILO disavowal — presenting the Philippines as an evidentiary void when the corpus holds a government-affiliated think tank paper with occupational-composition numbers. A second uncited institutional source quantifies the counterfactual that Section 5B currently asserts only through informality rates.
findings.evidence: [[discussion-paper-series-no-2020-29]] — Bayudan-Dacuycuy, Orbeta, Serafica & Baje (2020), PIDS Discussion Paper 2020-29, Philippine Institute for Development Studies, Dec 2020 (self-labelled preliminary and unreviewed). From the Oxford Internet Institute Online Labour Index, 2017-2020: creative-and-multimedia work is ~74% of Indonesia's online workforce and 47% of the Philippines' (vs 59% India, 52% Viet Nam), against ~20% globally where software development is nearly 50%; the Philippines and Indonesia are each under 5% of the global online workforce, while India, Bangladesh and Pakistan together are 52%; demand originates 47% in North America (US alone 40%), 24% Europe, 19% Asia; platform fees run 5-20%. Relevance caveat from the note: this is online freelancing/crowdwork, not social-media content creation. [[x-policy-issues-in-the-digital]] — ILO/ACT-EMP (2023), SEA employers' guide, citing World Bank 'Beyond Unicorns' (2021): Indonesian platform workers' 2019 monthly earnings were nearly 16% higher than other informal workers, at 49 hours/week versus 39 for the average worker and 38 for an informal worker, narrowing to about a 6% premium after controlling for hours. Note's caveat: location-based and freelancing gig work only, must not be repurposed as creator earnings.
findings.recommendation: Replace the Philippines row's 'Best available creator evidence' cell with the PIDS composition figures plus the wrong-population flag (creative-and-multimedia is 47% of Philippine and ~74% of Indonesian ONLINE FREELANCING work, not content creation), keeping the ILO disavowal as a second clause. Separately, add one clause to Section 5B's counterfactual sentence: Indonesian platform workers' 2019 earnings premium over other informal workers was ~16% gross, ~6% after controlling for the 49-vs-39-hour week — a quantified counterfactual, for gig work rather than creators. Displacement: the Vietnam/Singapore/Cambodia/Laos/Myanmar/Brunei/Timor-Leste row can be reduced to a one-line note under the table rather than a full table row.

findings.location: Section 5B, 'Four measured mechanisms of non-transfer' — convert the paragraph to a table (structural, but word-negative)
findings.issue: Per this run's directive on comparisons left in prose that belong in tables: Section 5B is the one place in the report where a set of parallel quantified comparisons runs as continuous prose while every peer section uses the four-field table format the decomposition requires. The paragraph carries four distinct comparisons, each with figures, thresholds and country tags — living-wage thresholds ($254.28 / $414.88 developing Asia vs $1,160 / $50,000 / $67,521 Western), RPM by audience market (~INR 30 vs $5 per 1,000 views at 70% fill), off-platform link infrastructure (India, Indonesia, Thailand over-represented among channels with no links), and the employment counterfactual (informality >70% Indonesia and Philippines, >60% Vietnam, 38% Thailand; ~71% of Indonesian e-commerce sellers social-only). None of these carries a visible sample size or year in the prose, though the sources supply them. This is also the cheapest place to recover words: tabulating removes the connective prose and would absorb the additions in findings 5 and 7 at roughly net zero.
findings.evidence: Report lines 150-152 (Section 5B), one paragraph of approximately 260 words carrying four comparisons and eight distinct figures, against Sections 1A, 2A, 2B, 4A, 5A, 5C and 5D which all present comparable material as tables. Sources already cited there: [[adbi-working-paper-series]], [[httpsdoiorg10117720563051241234693]], [[httpsdoiorg10117720563051231180628]], [[technologies]].
findings.recommendation: Convert to a five-column table: Mechanism | SEA/peripheral value | Western/core value | Gap | Source and year. Rows: living-wage threshold; revenue per 1,000 views; off-platform link prevalence; employment counterfactual (informality share); social-commerce composition. Flagged structural rather than surgical because it changes a paragraph into a table — hand to the orchestrator if the patcher cannot do it as one hunk. Expected effect on the word budget is negative, which is why it should be applied before findings 5 and 7.

findings.location: Section 6C provenance table, 'Southeast Asian income chain' column, or the paragraph at line 212
findings.issue: Section 6C traces the Indonesian 63% chain in detail and concludes it is citable with caveats. It does not mention that a competing Indonesian figure circulates simultaneously and points the opposite way — the '8 million creators but only 14% profiting' framing. Layer 1's coverage check flagged this pair explicitly and ruled that the two are not reconcilable and must not be presented as competing estimates of one quantity. Leaving the 14% unmentioned means the report silently resolves a live disagreement circulating in the Indonesian press in favour of the figure it happens to have traced, without stating that the other was checked and disqualified.
findings.evidence: [[ada-8-juta-kreator-konten-tapi-baru-14-persen-yang-cuan]] — Liputan6.com, 21 Aug 2023. The '8 million creators / 17 million by 2027 / $7bn cumulative income potential' figures are attributed to the IMF with no report, publication or link named anywhere in the article and none discoverable by search. The headline '14 percent' comes from a different source entirely — a cited 'studi Linktree', a self-selected vendor survey of active Linktree users with no sample size or scope given in the article — reporting that 59% of beginner creators have recorded no profit and only 14% have a built community and can profit. Neither figure specifies whether the population is Indonesian or global; the framing may in fact describe a global population. The same article quotes TipTip's CEO claiming 20 million creators on his own platform, unverified.
findings.recommendation: Add one clause to the line 212 paragraph: the competing '14% profiting' figure circulating in Indonesian coverage of the same 8-million headcount is a Linktree vendor survey of unstated (probably global) scope, not an Indonesian measurement, and cannot be differenced against the 63% — the two figures have different instruments, populations and denominators. One sentence; it forecloses the most obvious objection to the section's conclusion.

findings.location: Opening paragraph (line 3) and Section 6E 'What becomes measurable next'
findings.issue: Bloat check B2. The opening paragraph and the closing subsection make the same two claims in nearly the same words: that no platform-scale survival curve exists, and that no one has asked people who quit why they quit. The opener states 'Attrition has four measurements ... and no platform-scale survival curve' and 'Reasons for quitting have never been elicited from anyone who quit'; Section 6E closes with 'the two highest-value studies here remain unrun: a cohort survival curve over a full channel population, and an exit survey that asks people who stopped why they stopped — the second already half-built, since one US survey reaches a lapsed creator population and does not put the question to it.' Section 4C already carries the half-built point with the same source. Three passes over one observation at a length ceiling.
findings.evidence: Line 3 (opening paragraph), line 127 (Section 4C, the Sounds Profitable near-miss stated in full), line 220 (Section 6E, closing sentence restating both the absence and the near-miss). The Sounds Profitable source [[the-creators-2025-understanding-the-modern-podcast-creator-landscape-sounds-prof]] is cited at all three points for the same argument.
findings.recommendation: Cut the closing clause of Section 6E from '— the second already half-built' onward, since Section 4C states the near-miss with its full apparatus (n=5,034, 6% lapsed base, the open question left unasked). Keep Section 6E's genuinely forward-looking content, which the opener does not duplicate: the Internet Archive channel census (1.21bn captures, 106m+ channels), Indonesia's SE2026, and the 22nd ICLS standard due 2028. This recovers roughly 40 words toward the additions above.
